name: Question 8
problem: Consider the curve ${e}^{x}-{e}^{y}=y.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-3$ on the curve at the point where $y=0,$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}-{e}^{y} & =y \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{x}-{e}^{y}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{x})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{y}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({e}^{y}) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot {e}^{x}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot {e}^{y} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot {e}^{x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot ({e}^{y}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-3$ and $y=0.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)\cdot {e}^{x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot ({e}^{0}+1) \\ -3{e}^{x} & =2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $x,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $y=0$ into the equation of the curve.

At the point where $y=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}-{e}^{y} & =y \\ {e}^{x}-{e}^{0} & =0 \\ {e}^{x}-1 & =0 \\ {e}^{x} & =1 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{e}^{0} & =2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\ -3 & =2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
